newsitem.title: USA: Seagate acquires storage startup Quinta. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Seagate acquires storage startup Quinta. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]

text.p: Seagate Technology Inc said Wednesday it will acquire Quinta Corp., a 15-month old developer of high-capacity computer storage technology, in a deal analysts value at up to about $350 million.

Seagate, which has a minority stake in Quinta, said the start-up's other shareholders will receive a total of $230 million in cash and be eligible for further payments of up to $95 million linked to development and production milestones.
The move sets a high premium on the ability of a team of world-ranking engineers in the competitive disk drive market to create technologies which could lead to a leap forward in storage technology.

Quinta Chief Executive Steven Kitrosser said the company has developed such technology, which he predicted will enable storage of three to five times as much data on the same space as conventional disk drive technologies in coming years.
Quinta's optically assisted Winchester (OAW) technology was developed by a group of engineers which now comprise 55 of the 70 employees of the San Jose, Calif.-based company.

"We're in the process of developing a large patent protfolio of our own technology," Kitrosser said in a conference call with media. "We have a number of patents pending and continue to add to it every day."

Seagate, based in Scotts Valley, Calif., is the world's largest disk drive maker. The company expects a charge in the quarter in which the transaction closes of $180 million to $215 million to write off in-process research and development.
Seagate, whose stock added $1.75 to close at $36.75 on the New York Stock Exchange, said it anticipates an increase in demand for affordable, high-capacity on-line storage.
International Data Corp. (IDC) projects data storage cunsumption will surge from 76,000 terabytes in 1995 to nearly 3 million terabytes by the year 2000.

IDC analyst Crawford Del Prete said while the valuation may be rich, Quinta provides a fresh line of development which is likely to initially be introduced in high end storage devices and could eventually impact the entire industry.

Kitrosser said Quinta has "a relatively low-risk path" to more economical storage because it uses classic optical technology and diminishes the chance for damaging contact between the drive and the head used to read it.
Quinta executives said the company is prepared to announce its initial product later this year. (Corrects to clarify that the product is being made, not shipped.)

Quinta had raised more than $50 million from its lead venture capital firm of Sierra Ventures and subsequent investors, including Seagate, Read-Rite Corp., which will continue to be a supplier, and other venture groups.
Seagate Chairman and CEO Alan Shugart said the company initially plans to run Quinta as a separate, wholly owned subsidiary, taking advantage of synergies where possible.

"This is kind of like the Chinese taking over Hong Kong, " he said. "The only thing that really happened was the British flag came down and the Chinese flag went up and let's wait a couple of years and see how it works."
